patient.name: Priya Sharma
patient.complaint: Weight gain, a round red face and difficulty standing from a chair
background: No regular medication, drinks 4 units a week

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis/cause?' with weight gain plus the discriminating signs (proximal myopathy, purple striae, bruising); the drug or alcohol history usually decides the cause.

points: Priya, 38, sees her GP about **weight gain** over 18 months.
Her face has become **round and red**; rings no longer fit.
She struggles to **stand up from a low chair**.
Bruises appear with minor knocks; her periods are irregular.

steps.lead: Priya's changes span metabolism, blood pressure and body shape: one hormone links them, **excess cortisol**.

points: Exam: **moon face**, fat pad over the upper back (**buffalo hump**).
Wide **purple striae** across her abdomen; thin, easily bruised skin.
Proximal weakness: needs her arms to rise from squatting.
Thin arms and legs despite a large abdomen.

steps.lead: Priya has the full picture: **central obesity**, purple striae, proximal myopathy, bruising and new hypertension.

steps.q: Before any test, what must the GP ask Priya first?
o: Does she have a family history of diabetes?
Has she had recent weight-loss surgery?
Is she taking any steroid medication?
steps.r: **Exogenous corticosteroids** are the most common cause overall, so always exclude them first (tablets, inhalers, creams, injections).

points: No prednisolone, inhalers, steroid creams or joint injections.

steps.lead: Priya takes no steroids, so her cortisol is **endogenous**. Next question: ACTH-dependent or ACTH-independent?

steps.title: Causes of Cushing's syndrome
nodes: Exogenous steroids (most common overall) → ACTH low
Endogenous, ACTH-dependent: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) or ectopic ACTH
Endogenous, ACTH-independent: adrenal adenoma, carcinoma, hyperplasia
steps.caption: Cushing's **disease** means the pituitary source only; Cushing's **syndrome** is any cause.

steps.lead: Priya drinks little. A heavy drinker with the same picture may have **pseudo-Cushing's**: retest after a month off alcohol.
If Priya ever needed both adrenals removed, the unchecked pituitary adenoma could grow: **Nelson's syndrome**.

steps.text: Proximal myopathy, purple striae and easy bruising are the most **discriminating** features: obesity alone does not cause them.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial/next investigation?': low-dose dexamethasone to screen, then ACTH, high-dose testing and the right scan.

steps.lead: Priya's work-up follows three steps: **prove** cortisol excess (dexamethasone), **classify** it (ACTH), then **locate** it (imaging).

steps.title: GP bloods
steps.text: Low potassium, high bicarbonate and new diabetes all fit cortisol excess.

steps.lead: Priya takes **1 mg dexamethasone at 11pm**; her 8am cortisol should be suppressed. She takes no CYP450 inducers, so the test is valid.

visual.title: 8am cortisol after 1 mg overnight dexamethasone
visual.label: Priya 410
visual.caption: Normal people suppress below about 50 nmol/L. Priya does not: cortisol excess is likely.

steps.text: A second abnormal screen (24-hour urinary free cortisol, also high) confirms it.
A patient on **phenytoin, carbamazepine or rifampicin** clears dexamethasone fast and can 'fail' to suppress falsely. Use urinary or salivary cortisol instead.

steps.title: Classifying the cause
steps.text: ACTH not suppressed and both cortisol and ACTH fall with high-dose dexamethasone.

steps.lead: Priya's ACTH is high (ACTH-dependent) and both values suppress on **high-dose** testing: the pattern of a **pituitary adenoma**.

steps.q: Priya has ACTH-dependent Cushing's that suppresses on high-dose dexamethasone. Which scan next?
steps.r: ACTH-dependent with suppression points to the **pituitary**. CT adrenals is for ACTH-independent disease; CT chest hunts ectopic sources.

steps.lead: Priya's **pituitary MRI** shows a 6 mm microadenoma. Had her ACTH been low, an **adrenal CT** would have come next.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': wean exogenous steroids, metyrapone before surgery, or the definitive operation for the source.

steps.lead: Priya is not on steroids. Had her Cushing's been from prednisolone, the first step would be a **gradual wean**, never sudden withdrawal.
Stopping long-term steroids abruptly risks an **adrenal crisis**: shock, vomiting, hypotension and low sodium.

steps.text: Never answer 'stop the steroids immediately'. The answer is **reduce gradually** (or use the lowest dose that controls the underlying disease).

steps.lead: Priya's cortisol and blood pressure are high before surgery, so the endocrinologist starts **metyrapone** to block cortisol synthesis.

visual.title: Priya's cortisol on metyrapone
visual.caption: Metyrapone brings cortisol down so she is safer for surgery; it does not remove the tumour.

steps.lead: Priya's source is the pituitary, so the definitive treatment is **transsphenoidal surgery**. An adrenal tumour would need adrenalectomy.

steps.title: Definitive treatment by source
nodes: Ectopic ACTH → treat the tumour (e.g. small cell lung cancer)
steps.caption: Match the treatment to where the excess cortisol comes from.

points: Six weeks later Priya has transsphenoidal surgery.
Day 3: 9am cortisol undetectable, a sign of cure.
She goes home on **hydrocortisone** until her axis recovers.
Given sick-day rules and a steroid card.

steps.lead: Priya still has hypertension, diabetes and bone loss to treat: **antihypertensives, glucose control and bone protection**.
Priya's pathway follows the **Endocrine Society** guideline: exclude exogenous steroids, two screening tests, then ACTH and imaging.

steps.text: Low or undetectable cortisol after surgery is good news. It means the tumour is gone, so cover her with hydrocortisone while the axis wakes up.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: hypokalaemic alkalosis, why the high-dose test separates pituitary from ectopic ACTH, and adrenal crisis after steroid withdrawal.

steps.lead: Priya's thin limbs, striae and bruises are **catabolic** protein effects; her belly fat, diabetes and BP are **metabolic** effects.

steps.title: Why Priya looks the way she does
nodes: Protein breakdown → muscle wasting, thin skin, striae
Fat redistribution → moon face, buffalo hump

steps.lead: Priya's corticotroph adenoma still 'hears' cortisol a little, so a **high** dose of dexamethasone switches it down; an ectopic tumour ignores it.
At high levels cortisol acts on **mineralocorticoid receptors**, so Priya loses potassium and hydrogen ions: low K+, high bicarbonate.

visual.title: Priya's potassium
visual.label: Priya 3.2
visual.caption: Mild hypokalaemia; ectopic ACTH typically drives it far lower because cortisol levels are much higher.

steps.lead: Cortisol switches off Priya's **osteoblasts** and dampens immunity: she is at risk of osteoporotic fracture and infection.
Long-term steroids suppress the **HPA axis**, so the adrenals cannot restart instantly if the steroid stops.

visual.title: Loss of the cortisol rhythm
visual.caption: Normally cortisol is lowest at midnight. In Cushing's the **diurnal variation is lost**, which is why late-night salivary cortisol works.

steps.text: Cushing's **disease** is ACTH-high with suppression on high-dose dexamethasone; **ectopic ACTH** is very high ACTH, no suppression and marked hypokalaemia.

mcq.q: What is the most common overall cause of Cushing's syndrome?
mcq.r: Iatrogenic steroids are the commonest cause, so always exclude them first.

mcq.q: What is the most common endogenous cause in the notes?
mcq.r: The notes list a solitary **adrenal adenoma** as the most common endogenous cause.
Cortisol's mineralocorticoid action wastes K+ and H+.

mcq.q: Which condition mimics Cushing's in chronic alcohol excess?
What is the first-line screening test?
Adrenal adenoma on high-dose dexamethasone shows:
mcq.r: The adrenal makes cortisol autonomously; ACTH is already switched off.

mcq.q: Which drug invalidates the dexamethasone suppression test?
mcq.r: CYP450 inducers speed dexamethasone clearance and cause false failure to suppress.

mcq.q: Which drug controls cortisol before definitive surgery?

mcq.r: Remove the pituitary adenoma; bilateral adrenalectomy risks Nelson's syndrome.

mcq.q: Why does stopping long-term steroids abruptly cause adrenal crisis?
mcq.r: Chronic negative feedback leaves the adrenals unable to make cortisol at once.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the alcohol history is the clue.

points.p: Cushingoid features and biochemistry from chronic alcohol excess
Repeat testing after 1 month of abstinence

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a complication after a specific operation.

points.p: Follows bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's
Pituitary adenoma enlarges: headache, visual field defects
Managed with transsphenoidal surgery

prompts.q: How does Cushing's differ from simple obesity, PCOS and Conn's?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: which feature tips the balance?

points.p: Proximal myopathy and purple striae are not in simple obesity or PCOS
points.why: PCOS shares weight gain and irregular periods.

points.p: Conn's has hypertension and low K+ but no body habitus change

prompts.q: What is the first-line test, how is it done and what invalidates it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: dose, timing and the drug interaction.

points.p: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test
1 mg at 11pm, cortisol at 8am; Cushing's fails to suppress
Alternatives: 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol
CYP450 inducers (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin) invalidate it

prompts.q: How do ACTH and the high-dose test localise the cause?

points.p: ACTH low = ACTH-independent (adrenal or exogenous)
Pituitary adenoma: cortisol and ACTH both suppress on high dose
Ectopic ACTH: neither suppresses
Adrenal adenoma: cortisol not suppressed, ACTH suppressed
Pituitary MRI for ACTH-dependent, adrenal CT for ACTH-independent

prompts.q: How is Cushing's managed by cause?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the treatment to the source.

points.p: Exogenous: wean steroids gradually, never stop abruptly
Metyrapone to control cortisol before surgery
Pituitary: transsphenoidal surgery
Adrenal tumour: adrenalectomy; ectopic: treat the malignancy
Treat complications: hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis

prompts.q: Why does Cushing's cause hypokalaemia, osteoporosis and infection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each feature to a cortisol action.

points.p: High cortisol acts on mineralocorticoid receptors: K+ loss, alkalosis
Suppresses osteoblasts and increases bone resorption
Impairs immune function
Protein catabolism: muscle wasting, thin skin, striae

prompts.q: Why does the high-dose test work, and why does abrupt steroid withdrawal cause crisis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: feedback is the answer to both.

points.p: Corticotroph adenoma retains partial negative feedback, so high dose suppresses
Long-term steroids suppress the HPA axis
Adrenals cannot restart cortisol production immediately

glossary.Cushing's syndrome: Clinical state caused by prolonged excess cortisol from any source.
glossary.Cushing's disease: Cushing's syndrome caused specifically by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
glossary.cortisol: The main glucocorticoid hormone made by the adrenal cortex; raises glucose and BP.
glossary.ACTH: Adrenocorticotropic hormone, made by the pituitary; drives the adrenals to make cortisol.
glossary.ACTH-dependent: Cortisol excess driven by too much ACTH, from the pituitary or an ectopic tumour.
glossary.ACTH-independent: Cortisol made autonomously by the adrenal or given as a drug; ACTH is suppressed.
glossary.ectopic ACTH: ACTH made by a tumour outside the pituitary, usually small cell lung cancer or carcinoid.
glossary.exogenous: Coming from outside the body, such as prescribed steroid tablets.
glossary.moon face: Round, full, often red face from fat redistribution in cortisol excess.
glossary.buffalo hump: Fat pad over the upper back and base of the neck.
glossary.striae: Stretch marks; in Cushing's they are wide and purple.
glossary.proximal myopathy: Weakness of muscles near the trunk, such as hips and shoulders; hard to stand up.
glossary.central obesity: Fat gain around the abdomen and trunk with relatively thin limbs.
glossary.hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis: Low potassium with high blood bicarbonate, caused here by mineralocorticoid action.
glossary.pseudo-Cushing's: Cushing-like features and tests from chronic alcohol excess, resolving with abstinence.
glossary.Nelson's syndrome: Growth of a pituitary adenoma after bilateral adrenalectomy, causing pigmentation and mass effect.
glossary.Carney complex: Rare inherited syndrome of adrenal nodules, skin pigmentation and heart myxomas.
glossary.adrenal adenoma: Benign tumour of the adrenal cortex; the commonest endogenous cause of Cushing's.
glossary.dexamethasone: A potent synthetic steroid used to test whether cortisol production can be suppressed.
glossary.dexamethasone suppression test: Gives dexamethasone then measures cortisol; failure to suppress suggests Cushing's.
glossary.urinary free cortisol: Cortisol measured in a 24-hour urine collection; raised in Cushing's.
glossary.salivary cortisol: Late-night saliva cortisol; raised in Cushing's because the night-time dip is lost.
glossary.diurnal variation: The normal daily rhythm of cortisol: high in the morning, lowest at midnight.
glossary.CYP450 inducers: Drugs such as rifampicin and carbamazepine that speed up liver breakdown of other drugs.
glossary.metyrapone: Drug that blocks cortisol synthesis in the adrenal; used before surgery.
glossary.transsphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery performed through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
glossary.adrenalectomy: Surgical removal of an adrenal gland.
glossary.adrenal crisis: Life-threatening cortisol deficiency with shock, vomiting and low sodium.
glossary.HPA axis: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol, with negative feedback.
glossary.negative feedback: When a hormone switches off the signals that cause its own release.
glossary.corticotroph: The pituitary cell type that makes ACTH.
glossary.mineralocorticoid: Hormone like aldosterone that retains sodium and excretes potassium.
glossary.glucocorticoid: Steroid hormone like cortisol that affects glucose, protein, fat and immunity.
glossary.catabolic: Breaking down tissue, for example muscle protein.
glossary.hydrocortisone: Synthetic cortisol, used for replacement and in adrenal crisis.
glossary.small cell lung cancer: Aggressive lung cancer linked to smoking; the commonest source of ectopic ACTH.
glossary.carcinoid: Neuroendocrine tumour that can secrete hormones including ACTH.
glossary.plethoric: Red, flushed appearance of the face.
glossary.Conn's syndrome: Primary hyperaldosteronism: hypertension with low potassium from an aldosterone-secreting adrenal.
glossary.sick-day rules: Advice to double steroid replacement during illness to avoid adrenal crisis.

technique.stem: A 41 year old woman has an 18 month history of weight gain and difficulty climbing stairs. She bruises easily. She takes no regular medication. Her BP is 158/96 mmHg. She has a round face, a large abdomen with wide purple striae and thin arms and legs.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about weight gain: ask whether the specific signs of cortisol excess are there.
Proximal myopathy, bruising, purple striae and central obesity with thin limbs are the **discriminating** signs.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Endogenous cortisol excess: **Cushing's syndrome**.

elim: Causes weight gain and myopathy but not purple striae or bruising.
Central obesity and BP fit, but not striae, bruising or proximal weakness.
Weight gain and irregular periods, but no proximal myopathy or easy bruising.
Hypertension and low K+, but no change in body shape or skin.

steps.x: **A. Cushing's syndrome.** Rule: weight gain + proximal myopathy + purple striae + bruising = Cushing's until proven otherwise.

technique.stem: A 52 year old man has central obesity, purple abdominal striae and proximal muscle weakness. He takes no steroid medication. His BP is 164/98 mmHg. His GP wants to test for Cushing's syndrome.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: 'Initial investigation' means the screening test, not the localising one.
Classic Cushingoid signs with no exogenous steroid: endogenous cortisol excess must be **proven** first.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Screen with the **1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test**.

elim: Imaging comes after cortisol excess is proven and classified.
Used later to localise the source, not to screen.
Only once ACTH-dependent disease is confirmed; incidentalomas are common.
Classifies the cause after cortisol excess is proven, not first.

steps.x: **C. Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test.** Rule: prove (low-dose dex) → classify (ACTH) → locate (high-dose dex and imaging).

technique.stem: A 64 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken prednisolone 15 mg daily for 2 years. She has developed a round face, bruising and proximal muscle weakness. Her BP is 150/90 mmHg. Her arthritis is now well controlled on methotrexate.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of a clear cause: decide how to remove it safely.
Iatrogenic Cushing's from long-term prednisolone; a steroid-sparing drug now controls her arthritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wean the steroid gradually** so her suppressed HPA axis can recover.

elim: The cause is obvious: exogenous steroid. No tumour to find.
Used for endogenous cortisol excess before surgery, not iatrogenic disease.
Abrupt withdrawal after 2 years risks **adrenal crisis**.
Still a glucocorticoid; it does not remove the cause.

steps.x: **A. Gradually reduce the prednisolone.** Rule: exogenous Cushing's → wean, never stop abruptly.

technique.stem: A 60 year old man who smokes has a 2 month history of weight loss, weakness and swollen ankles. His BP is 172/100 mmHg. Bloods show potassium 2.4 mmol/L and bicarbonate 36 mmol/L. His 9am ACTH is very high and does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his hypokalaemia?

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain the abnormal result in this vignette.

clues: does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone
steps.x: Smoker, weight loss, very high ACTH, no suppression: **ectopic ACTH** (e.g. small cell lung cancer) with profound hypokalaemic alkalosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Huge cortisol levels overwhelm local inactivation and act on **mineralocorticoid receptors**.

elim: That is Conn's; ACTH would be normal, not very high.
No vomiting or diarrhoea in the stem; bicarbonate and BP point elsewhere.
No diuretic is mentioned.
Rare; does not explain very high ACTH.

steps.x: **B. Cortisol acting on mineralocorticoid receptors.** Rule: very low K+ with high bicarbonate in Cushing's = mineralocorticoid action of cortisol, worst in ectopic ACTH.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has gained 15 kg over a year, mostly around her abdomen. She has irregular periods and finds it hard to stand from a chair without using her arms. Her BP is 156/94 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm. She has a plethoric round face and violaceous abdominal striae.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Proximal myopathy and purple striae with hypertension mean cortisol excess. PCOS gives irregular periods and weight gain but not these signs.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: find the features obesity alone cannot explain.

clues: hard to stand from a chair
steps.x: Proximal myopathy and **violaceous (purple)** striae with hypertension and a plethoric moon face.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cortisol excess: **Cushing's syndrome**.

elim: No cold intolerance or slow pulse; does not cause violaceous striae.
Irregular periods and weight, but no proximal myopathy or purple striae.
Irregular periods, but expect galactorrhoea, not striae and myopathy.
Striae would be pale and there would be no proximal myopathy.

steps.x: **A. Cushing's syndrome.** Purple striae + proximal myopathy separate Cushing's from simple obesity and PCOS.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with COPD has taken prednisolone repeatedly over the past year. He has developed central weight gain, thin skin and easy bruising. His BP is 148/90 mmHg and pulse rate 76 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his presentation?
practice.e: Exogenous steroids are the most common cause and must be excluded before any endogenous work-up.

steps.x: A cause question: look for the drug history.
Repeated prednisolone courses for COPD exacerbations plus Cushingoid features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Exogenous corticosteroids**, the commonest cause of Cushing's.

elim: Commonest endogenous cause, but he has an obvious exogenous one.
Smoker, but no weight loss or severe hypokalaemia; steroids explain it.
Possible but far less likely than his prednisolone.
Needs chronic alcohol excess, not given.

steps.x: **C. Exogenous corticosteroid use.** Always check the drug chart first, including inhaled, topical and injected steroids.

practice.stem: A 47 year old man has central obesity, a round face and hypertension. He drinks 60 units of alcohol a week. His overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows failure of cortisol suppression. Six weeks after stopping alcohol, the test is normal and his features are improving.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Pseudo-Cushing's from chronic alcohol mimics Cushing's clinically and biochemically but resolves after abstinence.

steps.x: Diagnosis: what explains abnormal tests that recover?

clues: Six weeks after stopping alcohol, the test is normal
steps.x: Heavy alcohol use, failed suppression, then normal results after abstinence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Pseudo-Cushing's syndrome**: Cushingoid biochemistry without true HPA axis disease.

elim: Autonomous cortisol would not normalise with abstinence.
A pituitary adenoma would keep failing to suppress.
Would not resolve on stopping alcohol.
Follows bilateral adrenalectomy; not relevant.

steps.x: **E. Pseudo-Cushing's syndrome.** Alcohol + Cushingoid + recovers off alcohol = pseudo-Cushing's; retest after 1 month abstinence.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman had bilateral adrenalectomy 3 years ago for Cushing's disease that was not cured by pituitary surgery. She now has headaches, darkening of her skin and difficulty seeing cars on either side when driving. Her BP is 128/80 mmHg and pulse rate 72 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Without cortisol negative feedback the corticotroph adenoma enlarges, causing pigmentation and chiasmal compression.

steps.x: A diagnosis question after surgery: think of complications.

clues: difficulty seeing cars on either side
steps.x: Bilateral adrenalectomy removes cortisol feedback; the adenoma grows, making ACTH (pigment) and compressing the chiasm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Nelson's syndrome**.

elim: She takes replacement; pigment plus mass effect points to the pituitary.
Would present with shock and vomiting, not field loss.
Sudden thunderclap headache, not a gradual picture.
Needs alcohol excess; does not cause field defects.

steps.x: **C. Nelson's syndrome.** Bilateral adrenalectomy + pigmentation + visual field loss = Nelson's.

practice.stem: A 39 year old woman has weight gain, proximal myopathy and purple striae. Her BP is 160/98 mmHg and pulse rate 86 bpm. Her renal function is normal and she takes no medication.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood tests?
practice.e: High cortisol acts on mineralocorticoid receptors, causing hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; high K+ and low Na+ suggest Addison's.

steps.x: A finding question: name the diagnosis, then predict its blood picture.
Classic Cushing's signs with hypertension and no diuretic to confuse things.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cortisol's mineralocorticoid effect: **hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis**.

elim: Hyperparathyroidism, not cortisol excess.
That is mineralocorticoid deficiency, as in Addison's.
Cortisol raises glucose; it does not lower it.
Typical of Addison's disease, the opposite state.

steps.x: **D. Low potassium and high bicarbonate.** Cushing's = low K+, high bicarbonate, often high glucose.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man who smokes 40 cigarettes a day has lost 8 kg in 2 months. He has proximal weakness, ankle oedema and darkening of his skin. His BP is 170/100 mmHg and pulse rate 92 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his Cushing's syndrome?
practice.e: Very high ACTH with pigmentation, rapid onset and profound hypokalaemia in a smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer.

steps.x: A cause question: decide ACTH-dependent or independent, then which source.
Heavy smoker with weight loss: malignancy. Pigmentation means **high ACTH**. Rapid onset with severe hypokalaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ectopic ACTH**, most often from small cell lung cancer.

elim: ACTH-independent: ACTH would be low, so no pigmentation.
ACTH-independent; skin would not darken, and K+ fall is less dramatic.
No steroid history; ACTH would be suppressed.
Slower, milder; ACTH is not this high and weight loss is unusual.

steps.x: **C. Ectopic ACTH secretion.** Smoker + weight loss + pigmentation + very low K+ = ectopic ACTH.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman has a positive overnight dexamethasone suppression test and a raised 24-hour urinary free cortisol. She takes no medication. Her BP is 154/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Once two screening tests confirm cortisol excess, plasma ACTH decides whether to image the pituitary or adrenals.

steps.x: 'Next' investigation: where are we in the pathway?
Two abnormal screening tests: cortisol excess is **confirmed**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Now classify: **plasma ACTH** (dependent or independent).

elim: Choose the scan only after ACTH tells you adrenal or pituitary.
Another screening test; she already has two abnormal ones.
Too early; ACTH must show dependent disease first.
Tests for adrenal insufficiency, the opposite problem.

steps.x: **D. Plasma ACTH.** Prove → classify (ACTH) → locate.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has confirmed Cushing's syndrome. Her plasma ACTH is undetectable. She takes no steroid medication. Her BP is 150/92 mmHg and pulse rate 78 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
practice.e: Undetectable ACTH without exogenous steroids means an adrenal source, so image the adrenals with CT.

steps.x: An imaging question: let ACTH pick the organ.
Suppressed ACTH with no exogenous steroid = **ACTH-independent**, an adrenal source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Adrenal CT**.

elim: Looks for an ectopic ACTH source; her ACTH is suppressed.
Separates pituitary from ectopic ACTH; not needed when ACTH is low.
For ACTH-dependent disease only.
Not sensitive enough for adrenal lesions.

steps.x: **A. CT adrenal glands.** Low ACTH → adrenal CT; high ACTH → pituitary MRI.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has Cushing's disease from a 7 mm pituitary microadenoma. She is awaiting surgery. Her BP is 168/102 mmHg and her glucose is poorly controlled.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate medical treatment while she waits?
practice.e: Metyrapone inhibits steroid synthesis and controls cortisol before definitive surgery.

steps.x: A pre-operative medical control question.
Uncontrolled cortisol effects (BP, glucose) before definitive surgery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Metyrapone** blocks cortisol synthesis.

elim: First-line for prolactinoma, not cortisol excess.
A mineralocorticoid replacement; would worsen BP.
Adds more cortisol.
Somatostatin analogue for acromegaly.

steps.x: **D. Metyrapone.** Bridge to surgery with metyrapone.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has Cushing's disease. Investigations show a high plasma ACTH, cortisol suppression on high-dose dexamethasone and a 5 mm adenoma on pituitary MRI. Her BP is 150/94 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment?
practice.e: Transsphenoidal resection is definitive for Cushing's disease; bilateral adrenalectomy risks Nelson's syndrome.

steps.x: 'Definitive' means the curative treatment.
ACTH-dependent, suppresses on high dose, adenoma on MRI: pituitary source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transsphenoidal surgery** to remove the adenoma.

elim: Last resort; risks Nelson's syndrome.
Controls cortisol but does not remove the tumour.
For residual or recurrent disease after surgery.
For an adrenal adenoma, not a pituitary source.

steps.x: **D. Transsphenoidal surgery.** Pituitary Cushing's → transsphenoidal surgery; adrenal → adrenalectomy; ectopic → treat the tumour.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has taken prednisolone 20 mg daily for 3 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. He ran out 3 days ago. He is drowsy and vomiting. His pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 78/46 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Abrupt withdrawal of long-term steroids with a suppressed HPA axis causes adrenal crisis, treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids.

steps.x: Initial management of a shocked patient.
Long-term steroids suddenly stopped, now hypotensive and vomiting: **adrenal crisis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV hydrocortisone** with IV fluids.

elim: Less mineralocorticoid effect; hydrocortisone is standard in crisis.
Too slow and the wrong route in shock.
He is vomiting; oral absorption is unreliable in crisis.
